title: Teacher-student relationship and teaching styles in primary education. A model of analysis
venue: Journal of Professional Capital and Community
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teaching styles are associated with how students perceive their relationships with teachers, and whether those perceptions vary by student profile. The authors focus on two teaching styles—directive and participative—and two dimensions of the teacher-student relationship—emotional and educational. Their aim is to determine whether more participative teaching is linked to more positive student perceptions, and whether these patterns differ across student characteristics.

The study uses census data from the 2018/2019 Diagnostic Assessment of the Canary Islands, focusing on 21,126 sixth-grade primary students in Spain. The analysis relies on student questionnaire responses, with some family questionnaire information for demographic variables. The authors construct latent variables through confirmatory factor analysis and estimate a structural equation model to test associations between teaching styles and perceived teacher-student relationship, then compare means across subgroups by gender, relative age, and parental education.

The findings suggest that participative teaching is more strongly associated with positive emotional and educational relationships than directive teaching, though both styles are positively correlated with perceived relationship quality. Student perceptions also differ by gender and parental education: girls report stronger participative, emotional, and educational perceptions than boys, and students from lower parental education backgrounds tend to perceive directive style more clearly and often report stronger educational relationship ratings. The paper concludes that classroom experience is shaped by student background and that teaching style perceptions are heterogeneous, especially by family cultural capital.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed observational/correlational SEM study using cross-sectional census data, not an experiment or quasi-experiment. It has a clear methodology and large sample, but it does not establish causality and is not a target-domain AI intervention study.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant associations and small subgroup differences, but no causal impact estimate or intervention effect size meeting a modest-impact threshold. Its relevance for the requested AI-powered K-12 science causal-comparison evidence is indirect and therefore limited.

finding.finding_summary: This is a correlational SEM study of 21,126 sixth-grade students in the Canary Islands (2018/2019) examining how perceived teaching styles relate to perceived teacher-student relationship quality. The participative teaching style was more strongly associated with both emotional and educational relationship perceptions than the directive style; all standardized coefficients were significant at 1%, but no causal effect sizes were reported beyond model fit and mean differences (e.g., girls had small advantages, Cohen's d≈0.08-0.10 for participative/emotional/educational perceptions).
finding.measure: Student questionnaire latent factors for participative teaching style, directive teaching style, emotional teacher-student relationship, and educational teacher-student relationship

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the model can be replicated in other education systems and periodically reused with diagnostic-assessment data, but this is a methodological and policy-oriented claim rather than a tested intervention outcome. It reports that the latent constructs can be estimated from routine assessment questionnaires, yet no implementation trial or institutional outcome estimate is provided.
finding.measure: Feasibility of using diagnostic assessment questionnaires for recurrent system-level monitoring of teacher-student relationship perceptions
